newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-India's L&T order growth slows.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-India's L&T order growth slows.

text.p: Indian engineering and construction giant Larsen & Toubro Ltd (L&T) said on Thursday it recorded a 20 percent rise in new orders in the nine months ending on December 31, 1997.
Order backlog until the end of December amounted to more than 43.0 billion rupees, L&T's senior vice president (finance) and board member Yeshwant Deosthalee, said in an interview with Reuters.
"Twenty percent growth in fresh orders is not bad, but it doesn't seem to tally with the order backlog figure," said an analyst at a Bombay securities firm.
The order backlog included orders booked, but not executed, last year. Analysts said L&T had recorded new order growth of over 35 percent in 1995/96 (April-March).
"It is definitely a slowdown," said an equities analyst.

"Expectations of these people could have been higher," Deosthalee said, referring to securities firms which put a "sell" on L&T's shares saying the slowdown in new orders would impact on the company's sales during 1997/98.
Deosthalee said several of its clients continued to face funding problems in implementing new projects.
"Companies are finding problems in securing short-term funds," Deosthalee said. "Banks are saying credit offtake is poor, customers are saying banks are not giving funds."
He said some of L&T's customers, who had gone ahead with projects, have found gaps in funding.
This was true of the economy as a whole, he said.
"We are well-positioned to capture the economic opportunities but we can't be isolated (from the problems facing the economy)," Deosthalee said.
He said L&T, one of India's top 10 companies based on sales with a turnover of 43.23 billion rupees ($1.2 billion) in 1995/96, was better prepared than many others facing the challenges.
Deosthalee said demand growth in cement fell to around 10.0 percent in the second half of 1996/97 from 13.0 percent during the first half. L&T is one of India's top cement makers.
L&T planned to commission a jetty on the west coast which would facilitate shipping cement to southern India which analysts said could improve its margins.
Deosthalee attributed the slowdown in many segments of the economy to a liquidity shortage in 1995/96 and a downtrend in the capital markets which hurt firms' fund-raising ability.
L&T's new projects were substantially funded until the end of calendar 1998, he said. These include a new cement plant at Tadpatri in south India and two captive power plants.
Deosthalee said the company's debt equity ratio was very conservative at less than one to one. "It could be 0.75 to one by the year-end," he said.
